Consult Summary:
- 34-year-old female marathon trainee with 2-week history of activity-related right knee pain with audible clicking, intermittent swelling (transient), and one episode of right toe tingling after running.
- Management: conservative measures advised (ice, reduce running), referral to physiotherapy arranged, and a stronger oral anti-inflammatory to be sent to pharmacy (name/dose not documented); urgent review advised for persistent swelling, heat, fever, or locked knee.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Right knee pain — probable overuse/mechanical
- Onset/duration: symptoms began ~2 weeks ago; started after increasing longer runs over the past month while training for a marathon.
- Symptoms/progression: activity-related pain that typically begins ~20 minutes into running (~2.5–3 miles); audible clicking with flexion/extension during gym exercises; transient swelling noted after first problematic run, currently not swollen and not painful at rest.
- Systems review/pertinent negatives: no locking, no giving way, full range of motion reported, no problems walking or using stairs, no calf pain, no persistent redness or warmth.
- Relevant history: recent fall on ice months ago with a large bruise; otherwise no prior chronic joint problems.
- Examination findings: no clinician-performed exam documented.
- Differential/plan discussed: mechanical overuse injury vs internal knee pathology (e.g., cartilage/ligament injury); definitive diagnosis deferred pending physiotherapy assessment and possible imaging if indicated.
- Management given: advised regular icing; advised to reduce running if painful; permitted NSAID use; referral to physiotherapist recommended; clinician to send prescription for a stronger anti-inflammatory to pharmacy (name/dose not documented); urgent review arranged if persistent swelling/heat/redness, systemic symptoms, or knee locks.

Issue 2: Intermittent right toe tingling
- Timeline: single episode noted following a run (described as tingling in right toes), has resolved.
- Associated features/negatives: no persistent altered sensation, no change in color or temperature of lower leg, no calf pain, no ongoing numbness.
- Plan: observed; if paresthesia recurs or persists, advised to report for further assessment.

Issue 3: Analgesic and other medication/substance use
- Medications and use reported: intermittent ibuprofen (stated up to 400 mg sometimes), reports occasional use of “Aleve” (patient unsure of classification) — dose/route/frequency not documented for Aleve; vitamin D; melatonin; occasional Xanax for sleep when needed — dose/route/frequency not documented; occasional recreational cannabis use (“smoke a joint”).
- Advice given: clinician advised that a prescribed stronger anti-inflammatory should not be taken concurrently with ibuprofen and to take with food.
- Plan: prescription for stronger anti-inflammatory to be sent to pharmacy (name/dose not documented); medication reconciliation incomplete (see quality checks).

Medications:
- Ibuprofen — patient-reported use, up to 400 mg (patient-stated; dose/route/frequency not fully documented).
- Aleve — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient uncertain about drug class).
- Vitamin D — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Melatonin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Xanax (alprazolam) — occasional use; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Stronger anti-inflammatory to be prescribed by clinician — name/dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- No allergies documented in the consult.

Past Medical History:
- Farsightedness; prior LASIK surgery.
- Past severe UTI suspected as kidney stones requiring ER visit (no further details).
- Otherwise reports only routine minor illnesses (colds).

Social History:
- Lives at home (address provided).
- Active lifestyle: training for a marathon; running 4–8 miles per run; attends gym several times weekly; plays ice hockey.
- Recreational drug use: occasional cannabis (smokes a joint).
- No tobacco cigarette use, alcohol intake, or living arrangements beyond address were documented.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care items (cervical screening, mammogram, prostate testing, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, recent optometry/skin check) were documented.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs recorded.
- No clinician physical examination findings documented in the transcript.

Plan:
- Conservative self-care: continue icing the knee regularly; reduce running volume and avoid runs that cause pain.
- Pharmacologic: clinician to send prescription for a stronger anti-inflammatory to the patient’s pharmacy (name/dose/route/frequency not documented); advised not to combine with ibuprofen and to take with food.
- Allied health referral: referral to physiotherapy arranged for formal assessment and management.
- Imaging: to be considered if physiotherapist or clinician assessment indicates possible intra-articular/cartilage or ligament injury.
- Safety/urgent advice: return for urgent review if persistent swelling, increased warmth/redness, fever, feeling systemically unwell, or if the knee becomes locked and cannot bend/straighten.
- Follow-up: physiotherapy assessment as first-line; clinic appointment available if physiotherapy wait is prolonged.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No clinician physical examination findings documented (no knee exam performed on video).
  - No vital signs recorded.
  - Exact name, dose, route, and frequency of the stronger anti-inflammatory were not documented.
  - Full medication reconciliation lacking (overlap/confusion regarding Aleve vs acetaminophen noted by patient).
  - No imaging results (none performed).
  - No allergy list confirmed (patient did not state allergies).
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Initial statement suggests "knees" (plural) hurting and clicking; later patient clarifies pain is in the right knee only — conflict noted.
  - Patient named “Aleve” then expressed uncertainty about its drug class (patient thought it might be acetaminophen) — inconsistency noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Conversation generally clear and audible; minimal background noise; some informal language and patient uncertainty about medication names/doses.
